items.name: $100M Offers
items.big: Make an offer so good people feel stupid saying no.
ideas: Value = (dream outcome × how likely it feels) ÷ (time it takes × effort and sacrifice). Raise the top, shrink the bottom.
Sell to a starving crowd: people with a painful problem, money to spend, easy to reach, in a growing market.
Don't compete on price. Charge more and deliver far more; low prices attract the worst customers.
Stack bonuses, add guarantees, scarcity and urgency, and name the offer clearly.
items.use: Use it when you decide what to sell and how to price it.

items.name: $100M Leads
items.big: There are only four ways to get customers: warm outreach, cold outreach, free content, and paid ads.
ideas: Start with warm outreach (people who know you), then add content, cold outreach and ads as you grow.
Give away so much value for free that people want to pay for more.
A 'lead magnet' solves one small problem for free and shows the next problem your product solves.
Do more of what works. Volume beats cleverness at the start (the 'rule of 100': 100 actions a day).
items.use: Use it when you need more people to see and buy your product.

items.name: The Lean Startup
items.big: Build the smallest thing that tests your idea, measure what happens, learn, repeat.
ideas: Build–Measure–Learn: every product is an experiment until customers prove it works.
A minimum viable product (MVP) is the cheapest way to test if people will actually pay.
Measure real behavior (sales, repeat buyers), not 'vanity metrics' like likes.
Pivot or persevere: change direction when the data says so, not when you get bored.
items.use: Use it when testing products in your store: small tests before big spending.

items.name: The Mom Test
items.big: Everyone lies to you about your idea to be nice, so ask about their life, not your idea.
ideas: Ask about what people did in the past, not what they would do in the future.
Talk about their problem and what they already spent money on to solve it.
Compliments are worthless; commitments (time, money, a pre-order) are real signals.
items.use: Use it before choosing a product: talk to real buyers first.

items.name: Zero to One
items.big: The best businesses create something new instead of copying what already exists.
ideas: Competition kills profits; aim to be the only one doing your thing for a specific group.
Start small and dominate a niche, then expand.
Ask: what important truth do very few people agree with you on?
items.use: Use it when thinking about your bigger, long-term business.

items.name: The E-Myth Revisited
items.big: Work on your business, not just in it: build systems so it runs without you doing everything.
ideas: Most people who start businesses are technicians who end up with a job, not a business.
Write down how every task is done, so someone else (or software) can do it.
Imagine your business as a franchise prototype: the same great result every time.
items.use: Use it when the store grows and you can't do everything yourself.

items.name: Profit First
items.big: Take your profit first, then run the business on what's left.
ideas: Sales − Profit = Expenses, not Sales − Expenses = Profit.
Split money into separate accounts right away: profit, owner pay, tax, operating costs.
Having less to spend forces you to be creative and efficient.
items.use: Use it as soon as money starts coming in, so you keep some of it.

items.name: The Psychology of Money
items.big: Doing well with money is more about behavior than intelligence.
ideas: Compounding is the most powerful force in money: time matters more than returns.
Wealth is what you don't see: the money you didn't spend.
'Enough' is a skill. Never risk what you have and need for what you don't have and don't need.
Leave room for error: save more than seems necessary.
items.use: Use it to build good money habits for life.

items.name: The Richest Man in Babylon
items.big: Keep at least a tenth of everything you earn. Pay yourself first.
ideas: Save at least 10% of all income before spending anything.
Make your saved money work: invest it so it earns more money.
Guard your savings from risky 'too good to be true' deals.
Increase your ability to earn by learning skills.
items.use: Use it as the simplest money rule to start with.

items.name: Rich Dad Poor Dad
items.big: The rich buy assets that put money in their pocket; most people buy liabilities that take it out.
ideas: An asset puts money in your pocket; a liability takes money out.
Learn financial skills early: school rarely teaches them.
Work to learn, not only to earn.
items.use: Use it for the asset vs liability mindset.
items.note: Great for mindset, but some advice (like heavy use of debt) is risky. Take the mindset, not the tactics.

items.name: The Millionaire Next Door
items.by: Thomas J. Stanley & William D. Danko
items.big: Most real millionaires live below their means and look ordinary.
ideas: Spending on status symbols is the enemy of becoming wealthy.
Wealth comes from earning well, spending less, and investing the difference for years.
items.use: Use it when you start making money and feel like spending it on flashy things.

items.name: The Intelligent Investor
items.big: Invest with a margin of safety, and don't let the market's mood control you.
ideas: Think of the market as 'Mr. Market': a moody partner offering prices every day. Use him, don't obey him.
Buy with a margin of safety: pay much less than something is worth.
Investing is thorough analysis, safety of principal, and an adequate return; anything else is speculation.
items.use: Use it when you're ready to invest profits (with a parent, since you're under 18).

items.name: The Little Book of Common Sense Investing
items.big: Buy the whole market cheaply with index funds and hold for decades.
ideas: Most professional investors don't beat the market after fees.
Low-cost index funds let you own a piece of every big company.
Costs and taxes matter enormously over time; keep them low.
items.use: Use it for the simplest long-term investing plan.

items.name: Influence
items.big: People say yes for predictable reasons.
ideas: Reciprocity: give first and people want to give back.
Commitment and consistency: small yeses lead to bigger ones.
Social proof: people follow what others do (reviews, numbers of buyers).
Authority, liking, scarcity and unity also push people to say yes. Use them honestly.
items.use: Use it on product pages and ads: reviews, limited stock, guarantees.

items.name: Never Split the Difference
items.big: Negotiation is about understanding the other side's emotions, not tricking them.
ideas: Tactical empathy: show you understand how they feel ('It seems like…').
Ask calibrated 'how' and 'what' questions: 'How am I supposed to do that?'
Mirroring: repeat their last few words to get them to say more.
Aim for 'That's right', not a quick 'yes'.
items.use: Use it when talking to suppliers about prices and shipping.

items.name: How to Win Friends and Influence People
items.big: People care most about themselves: show real interest in them.
ideas: Remember names and make people feel important, sincerely.
Don't criticize, condemn or complain.
Talk in terms of what the other person wants.
items.use: Use it with customers, suppliers, partners and everyone else.

items.name: Building a StoryBrand
items.big: Your customer is the hero of the story; your brand is the guide.
ideas: Clearly say what you offer, how it makes life better, and what to do to buy.
Every customer story: a hero with a problem meets a guide who gives a plan and calls them to act.
Confusing messages lose sales. Clarity wins.
items.use: Use it when writing your store's homepage and product pages.

items.name: This Is Marketing
items.big: Find the smallest group of people you can truly delight, and serve them.
ideas: People like us do things like this: marketing is about belonging.
Pick your smallest viable audience instead of trying to reach everyone.
Marketing is helping people become who they want to become.
items.use: Use it when choosing your niche and your personal brand's audience.

items.name: Purple Cow
items.big: Be remarkable (worth making a remark about) or be invisible.
ideas: Safe and boring products get ignored.
Design something so interesting that people talk about it.
items.use: Use it to test product ideas: would anyone share this?

items.name: Contagious
items.big: Things spread when they hit six triggers: social currency, triggers, emotion, public, practical value, stories.
ideas: People share what makes them look good (social currency).
High-arousal emotions (awe, excitement, even anger) get shared most.
Useful tips and stories carry a product along with them.
items.use: Use it when planning viral content and TikTok ads.

items.name: Made to Stick
items.big: Sticky ideas are Simple, Unexpected, Concrete, Credible, Emotional Stories.
ideas: Find the core of your message and cut the rest.
Concrete details beat abstract claims ('holds 20 kg', not 'super strong').
items.use: Use it when writing ad hooks and product descriptions.

items.name: Ogilvy on Advertising
items.big: Advertising should sell, not just look creative.
ideas: The headline does most of the work: most people read only the headline.
Specific facts sell better than general claims.
Test everything and keep what sells.
items.use: Use it when writing ads and product titles.

items.name: Breakthrough Advertising
items.big: You can't create desire; you can only channel desire that already exists.
ideas: Match your message to how aware the customer is: of the problem, of solutions, of your product.
The more crowded the market, the more specific and new your promise must be.
items.use: Use it when your ads stop working and you need a new angle.

items.name: Traction
items.big: There are 19 ways to get customers; test several and double down on the best one.
ideas: Bullseye: brainstorm all channels, test the most promising 3 cheaply, focus on the winner.
Spend half your time on getting customers, not just on the product.
items.use: Use it to choose where to find customers beyond one ad platform.

items.name: Good to Great
items.big: Great companies focus on what they can be best at, love doing, and can make money from.
ideas: The Hedgehog Concept: the overlap of passion, being best in the world, and your economic engine.
The flywheel: success comes from consistent pushes in one direction, not one big moment.
First who, then what: the right people matter before the right plan.
items.use: Use it when building a bigger business later.

items.name: The Hard Thing About Hard Things
items.big: There's no recipe for hard problems; the job is to keep going and make the tough calls.
ideas: The struggle is normal; every founder feels it.
Tell the truth fast, especially bad news.
items.use: Use it when things go wrong and you want to quit.

items.name: Shoe Dog
items.big: Nike started as a young guy selling imported shoes from his car. Keep going.
ideas: Phil Knight began by importing shoes from Japan and selling them himself: a lot like dropshipping.
Cash flow nearly killed Nike many times: growing fast needs money management.
Build a brand people love, not just a product.
items.use: Use it for inspiration: the most exciting business story for a young founder.

items.name: The 4-Hour Workweek
items.big: Design a business that runs without you, so you can live where and how you want.
ideas: DEAL: Definition, Elimination, Automation, Liberation.
80/20: find the 20% of work that gives 80% of results and cut the rest.
A 'muse' is a small automated product business that pays for your freedom.
items.use: Use it when you want the business to fund travel and freedom.

items.name: The Millionaire Fastlane
items.big: Wealth comes fastest from building a business that can reach many people, not from saving a salary for 40 years.
ideas: CENTS: Control, Entry (hard to copy), Need, Time (runs without you), Scale.
Solve a real need for many people and money follows.
items.use: Use it to judge whether a business idea can grow big.
items.note: Some parts are harsh about 'slow' saving; long-term investing still matters.

items.name: The Almanack of Naval Ravikant
items.big: Seek wealth, not money or status: own things that earn while you sleep.
ideas: Specific knowledge: what you're uniquely good at and love, which can't easily be taught.
Leverage: code, media (content) and capital let small teams have huge results.
Play long-term games with long-term people: trust compounds like money.
You won't get rich renting out your time.
items.use: Use it for the big picture: why a personal brand is powerful.

items.name: The Personal MBA
items.big: Every business does five things: creates value, markets it, sells it, delivers it, and manages the money.
ideas: If any of the five parts is missing, it's not a business.
You can learn most of business school from books, cheaply.
items.use: Use it as a map of the whole business.

items.name: Built to Sell
items.big: Build a business that could be sold one day, even if you never sell it.
ideas: Focus on one thing you do very well and can teach others to do.
A business that depends on you is hard to sell and hard to enjoy.
items.use: Use it when turning your store into a real brand.

items.name: Company of One
items.big: Bigger isn't always better: a small, profitable business can give you freedom.
ideas: Grow only when growth makes the business better, not just bigger.
Stay lean: fewer costs mean more profit and more freedom.
items.use: Use it when deciding whether to hire or scale.

items.name: Blue Ocean Strategy
items.big: Don't fight in a crowded 'red ocean'; create new space where competition doesn't matter.
ideas: Eliminate, reduce, raise, create: change what your product offers compared to everyone else.
Find what customers put up with and remove it.
items.use: Use it when every product in your niche looks the same.

items.name: Atomic Habits
items.big: Tiny improvements, done every day, add up to huge results.
ideas: Get 1% better every day.
Focus on systems (what you do daily) rather than goals.
Make good habits obvious, attractive, easy and satisfying.
Identity first: 'I'm the kind of person who logs my numbers every day.'
items.use: Use it to stick with training, logging and learning every day.

items.name: Deep Work
items.big: Focused, distraction-free work is rare and extremely valuable.
ideas: Block time with no phone and no notifications.
Shallow busywork feels productive but moves little.
items.use: Use it when you need to build something important after school.

items.name: Principles
items.big: Pain + reflection = progress. Write down your principles and improve them.
ideas: Embrace reality and deal with it.
Be radically open-minded: look for where you might be wrong.
Mistakes are lessons; write down what you learned.
items.use: Use it when you make mistakes and want to learn faster.

items.name: Show Your Work!
items.big: Share your process as you learn, and an audience will find you.
ideas: You don't have to be a genius; share what you're learning.
Teach what you know: it builds trust.
Be consistent: share something small every day.
items.use: Use it to start your personal brand right now, safely.

items.name: Crushing It!
items.big: Anyone can build a personal brand today by making lots of useful content on the right platforms.
ideas: Document, don't create: film your journey instead of inventing content.
Pick platforms where your audience's attention is, and post a lot.
items.use: Use it when you start your personal brand content.

items.name: Poor Charlie's Almanack
items.big: Learn the big ideas from many subjects and use them together to think clearly.
ideas: Mental models: a latticework of ideas from many fields.
Invert, always invert: ask how to fail, then avoid it.
Know your circle of competence and stay inside it.
items.use: Use it to make better decisions of any kind.

items.name: Warren Buffett
items.big: Buy wonderful businesses at fair prices and hold them for a very long time.
ideas: Rule No. 1: never lose money. Rule No. 2: never forget rule No. 1.
Look for a moat: something that protects a business from competitors.
Be fearful when others are greedy and greedy when others are fearful.
Stay inside your circle of competence.
items.fun: Started selling gum, soda and newspapers as a kid; bought his first stock at 11.

items.name: Charlie Munger
items.big: Avoid stupidity rather than trying to be brilliant.
ideas: Invert: figure out what would ruin you and avoid it.
Use mental models from many fields.
Be patient: the big money is in waiting.

items.name: Naval Ravikant
items.big: Build or buy equity in things that earn without your time.
ideas: Specific knowledge + leverage + accountability = wealth.
Read what you love until you love to read.
Productize yourself.

items.name: Alex Hormozi
items.big: Make offers so good people feel stupid saying no, then get in front of a lot of people.
ideas: Volume negates luck: do more reps than anyone.
Price on value, not on cost.
Give value for free until people ask how to pay you.

items.name: Paul Graham
items.big: Make something people want.
ideas: Do things that don't scale at the start: talk to every customer yourself.
Launch fast and improve based on real users.
The best ideas often look like toys at first.

items.name: Jeff Bezos
items.big: Obsess over customers, not competitors.
ideas: Focus on what won't change: people will always want low prices, fast delivery and big selection.
Regret minimization: at 80, which choice will you regret not making?
Stay 'Day 1': keep the energy of a startup.
items.fun: Started Amazon selling books from his garage.

items.name: Steve Jobs
items.big: Focus means saying no to a hundred good ideas.
ideas: Simplicity is the ultimate sophistication.
Start with the customer experience and work back to the technology.
Stay hungry, stay foolish.

items.name: Elon Musk
items.big: Reason from first principles, not by copying what others do.
ideas: Break a problem down to the basic facts and rebuild it from there.
Work on things that matter at huge scale.
items.fun: Sold a video game he coded at 12 for about $500.

items.name: Sara Blakely
items.big: Start with the little money you have, and see failure as a sign you tried.
ideas: Started Spanx with about $5,000 of savings.
Don't share your idea with doubters too early; build first.
Her dad asked every night: 'What did you fail at this week?'

items.name: MrBeast (Jimmy Donaldson)
items.big: Obsess over what makes people click and keep watching, then reinvest everything.
ideas: The title and thumbnail decide if anyone watches: make them irresistible.
Reinvest profits into making the next thing better.
He studied his craft for years before it took off.

items.name: Gary Vaynerchuk
items.big: Attention is the asset: go where people's attention is now.
ideas: Document your journey instead of trying to look perfect.
Patience plus hard work beats shortcuts.
Started a trading-card and lemonade hustle as a kid.

items.name: Seth Godin
items.big: Be remarkable to a small group who cares, instead of average to everyone.
ideas: Find your smallest viable audience.
Ship your work, even if it isn't perfect.

items.name: Peter Thiel
items.big: Competition is for losers: build something unique.
ideas: Dominate a small market first.
Look for secrets: truths few people see.

items.name: Ray Dalio
items.big: Pain plus reflection equals progress.
ideas: Write down your principles.
Diversify: don't bet everything on one thing.

items.name: Morgan Housel
items.by: Author of The Psychology of Money
items.big: Saving money is the gap between your ego and your income.
ideas: Time is the most powerful force in money.
Stay reasonable, not perfectly rational.

items.name: Phil Knight
items.big: Let everyone else call your idea crazy. Just keep going.
ideas: Began by importing shoes and selling from his car.
Built a brand around athletes and emotion, not just shoes.

items.name: Sam Walton
items.big: Keep costs low and pass the savings to customers.
ideas: Visit competitors and copy their best ideas.
Listen to everyone, especially the people on the front line.
items.fun: Delivered newspapers and sold magazines as a kid.

items.name: Andrew Carnegie
items.big: Surround yourself with people smarter than you, and give back.
ideas: Spent the second half of his life giving his fortune away: libraries, schools.
Put your eggs in one basket and watch that basket closely.

items.name: Benjamin Franklin
items.big: An investment in knowledge pays the best interest.
ideas: A penny saved is a penny earned.
Daily self-review: he tracked 13 virtues every day.

items.name: Oprah Winfrey
items.big: Turn your real story into your brand, and own what you build.
ideas: Owning her show's production company made her a billionaire, not just being on TV.
Authenticity builds trust with an audience.
